name: Anthropic AI-resistant technical evaluations
citation: Primary: Tristan Hume (a lead on Anthropic's performance optimization team), 'Designing AI-resistant technical evaluations', Anthropic Engineering blog, published 21 January 2026, https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/AI-resistant-technical-evaluations. Secondary: Russell Brandom, 'Anthropic has to keep revising its technical interview test as Claude improves' (URL slug: '...so you can't cheat on it with Claude'), TechCrunch, 22 January 2026, https://techcrunch.com/2026/01/22/anthropic-has-to-keep-revising-its-technical-interview-test-so-you-cant-cheat-on-it-with-claude
evidence_tier: Primary company statement (Anthropic engineering blog, first-person practitioner account by the test's designer). TechCrunch is secondary press summarising that post.
access_status: Anthropic post fully read (full page text retrieved and quotes checked by text search). TechCrunch article read via a fetch summary; its quotes are reproductions of the Anthropic post, plus its own correction note.
sponsor_and_incentive: Anthropic sells Claude and Claude Code; a post saying its model matches top human candidates also showcases the product's capability. The post doubles as recruiting (open challenge with a recruiting email address). Same company as Felix Rieseberg's statements, so not independent corroboration.
exact_quotes: "Since early 2024, our performance engineering team has used a take-home test where candidates optimize code for a simulated accelerator. Over 1,000 candidates have completed it, and dozens now work here, including engineers who brought up our Trainium cluster and shipped every model since Claude 3 Opus. But each new Claude model has forced us to redesign the test." (Anthropic post, opening section)

"When given the same time limit, Claude Opus 4 outperformed most human applicants. That still allowed us to distinguish the strongest candidates—but then Claude Opus 4.5 matched even those. Humans can still outperform models when given unlimited time, but under the constraints of the take-home test, we no longer had a way to distinguish between the output of our top candidates and our most capable model." (Anthropic post, opening section; note the original contains an em dash, keep it verbatim only inside quotation marks)

"By May 2025, Claude 3.7 Sonnet had already crept up to the point where over 50% of candidates would have been better off delegating to Claude Code entirely. I then tested a pre-release version of Claude Opus 4 on the take-home. It came up with a more optimized solution than almost all humans did within the 4-hour limit." (section 'Then Claude Opus 4 defeated it')

"I watched Claude Code work on the problem for 2 hours, gradually improving its solution. It solved the initial bottlenecks, implemented all the common micro-optimizations, and met our passing threshold in under an hour. Then it stopped, convinced it had hit an insurmountable memory bandwidth bottleneck." (section 'Then Claude Opus 4.5 defeated that')

"When I told Claude the cycle count it was possible to achieve, it thought for a while and found the trick. ... By the 2-hour mark, its score matched the best human performance within that time limit—and that human had made heavy use of Claude 4 with steering. We tried it out in our internal test-time compute harness for more rigor and confirmed it could both beat humans in 2 hours and continue climbing with time." (same section)
"We were about to release a model where the best strategy on our take-home would be delegating to Claude Code." (same section)

"Some colleagues suggested banning AI assistance. I didn't want to do this. Beyond the enforcement challenges, I had a sense that given people continue to play a vital role in our work, I should be able to figure out some way for them to distinguish themselves in a setting with AI— like they'd have on the job." (section 'Considering the options')

"A human trying to steer Claude would likely be constantly behind, understanding what Claude did only after the fact. The dominant strategy might become sitting back and watching." (section 'Considering the options')

"Nowadays performance engineers at Anthropic still have lots of work to do, but it looks more like tough debugging, systems design, performance analysis, figuring out how to verify the correctness of our systems, and figuring out how to make Claude's code simpler and more elegant. Unfortunately these things are tough to test in an objective way without a lot of time or common context." (section 'Considering the options')

"Anthropic's general candidate guidance asks candidates to complete take-homes without AI unless indicated otherwise. For this take-home, we explicitly indicate otherwise. Longer-horizon problems are harder for AI to solve completely, so candidates can use AI tools (as they would on the job) while still needing to demonstrate their own skills." (section on design goals)

"Unlike Zachtronics games, I intentionally provided no visualization or debugging tools. ... Building debugging tools is part of what's being tested ... Judgment about how to invest in tooling is part of the signal." (section 'Attempt 2: Going weirder')

"Early results are promising: scores correlate well with the caliber of candidates' past work, and one of my most capable colleagues scored higher than any candidate so far. I'm still sad to have given up the realism and varied depth of the original. But realism may be a luxury we no longer have. The original worked because it resembled real work. The replacement works because it simulates novel work." (end of 'Attempt 2')

"Over the next year and a half, about 1,000 candidates completed the take-home, and it helped us hire most of our current performance engineering team. It proved especially valuable for candidates with limited experience on paper: several of our highest-performing engineers came directly from undergrad" (section 'Early results')
"We're curious how long it lasts." (closing line)

TechCrunch correction: "An earlier version of this article misstated Anthropic's policy towards the use of AI tools on the take-home test. In fact, AI use is expressly permitted." [TechCrunch wording via fetch summary]
date_and_recency: Anthropic post published 21 January 2026; TechCrunch 22 January 2026. Covers the take-home from its origin (November 2023, used from early 2024) to the Claude Opus 4.5 launch period (late 2025). Model claims refer to Claude 3.7 Sonnet (by May 2025), pre-release Claude Opus 4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and pre-release and launched Claude Opus 4.5. Ten months old at time of research (November 2026); newer models may change the picture.
key_claims: 1) Anthropic's performance engineering take-home (optimise code for a simulated accelerator) was predictive and helped hire most of the current performance engineering team. 2) Each new Claude model forced a redesign: Opus 4 beat most applicants within the 4-hour limit; Opus 4.5 matched the best human within the 2-hour limit of version 2. 3) Under the take-home's time constraints, Anthropic 'no longer had a way to distinguish between the output of our top candidates and our most capable model'; humans still win with unlimited time. 4) Hume rejected banning AI (enforcement problems, and wanting candidates to distinguish themselves 'in a setting with AI ... like they'd have on the job') and rejected simply raising the bar above Claude-alone (the dominant strategy might become 'sitting back and watching'). 5) A first redesign around a harder, realistic optimisation problem (2D TPU register transposition avoiding bank conflicts) failed because Claude drew on prior experience. 6) Version 3 uses out-of-distribution Zachtronics-style puzzles on a tiny, heavily constrained instruction set, optimised for minimal instruction count, with no debugging or visualisation tools supplied, so tooling judgement is part of the signal. It trades realism for novelty: 'The original worked because it resembled real work. The replacement works because it simulates novel work.' 7) The real job now looks more like debugging, systems design, performance analysis, verification and simplifying Claude's code, which are hard to test objectively in a short format. 8) The original take-home was released as an open challenge; beat 1487 cycles and email recruiting.
headline_figures: "Over 1,000 candidates have completed it" / "about 1,000 candidates completed the take-home" over roughly a year and a half from early 2024; "dozens now work here".
"over 50% of candidates would have been better off delegating to Claude Code entirely": Claude 3.7 Sonnet, by May 2025, on the original 4-hour version.
Original time limit 4 hours; version 2 cut to 2 hours (partly because scheduling overhead caused 'multi-week delays').
Pre-release Claude Opus 4: 'a more optimized solution than almost all humans did within the 4-hour limit'.

Pre-release Claude Opus 4.5 in Claude Code: met the passing threshold 'in under an hour'; by 2 hours matched the best human performance within that limit, after being told the achievable cycle count. That best human 'had made heavy use of Claude 4 with steering'.

Published benchmarks on the released challenge (clock cycles, lower is better): 2164 Claude Opus 4 after many hours in the test-time compute harness; 1790 Claude Opus 4.5 in a casual Claude Code session, 'approximately matching the best human performance in 2 hours'; 1579 Opus 4.5 after 2 hours in the harness; 1548 Claude Sonnet 4.5 after many more than 2 hours of test-time compute; 1487 Opus 4.5 after 11.5 hours in the harness; 1363 Opus 4.5 in an improved harness after many hours.

Challenge threshold: below 1487 cycles ('beating Claude's best performance at launch'). The fastest human solution ever submitted 'substantially exceeds' Claude's best with extensive test-time compute (no number given).
sample_and_method: Practitioner account, not a study. About 1,000 software/performance engineering candidates took the take-home over ~18 months. Model comparisons are the author's own runs of pre-release and released Claude models (in Claude Code sessions and in an internal test-time compute harness), scored by cycle count against the human score distribution. Some Opus 4.5 runs had a human hint (target cycle count). Version 3 validity claim rests on early, unquantified results and colleague testing. Subjects are software engineers (performance engineering roles).
what_is_measured: Original: performance optimisation skill on a realistic task (parallel tree traversal on a simulated accelerator, progressing through multicore, SIMD and VLIW packing; version 1 also included a bug to debug), with design goals of representing real work, high signal, no specific domain knowledge, and compatibility with AI use. Version 3: problem solving on novel, out-of-distribution work (minimal-instruction puzzles on a constrained instruction set), including judgement about how much to invest in building one's own debugging tools. Hume says the real job increasingly involves debugging, systems design, performance analysis, verification and simplifying Claude's code, which the take-home does not directly measure.
ai_policy_in_interview: AI permitted (explicitly, overriding Anthropic's general no-AI take-home guidance), with an AI-resistant redesign. Banning AI was considered and rejected. TechCrunch initially misstated the policy and corrected it: 'AI use is expressly permitted.'
scope_and_status: Rolled out for Anthropic's performance engineering team hiring (one team, not company-wide). Version 3 is the current 'Claude-resistant' take-home used in the typical process; the original is public as an open challenge.
validity_evidence: No criterion-validity coefficients. Anecdotal: the test 'proved predictive' (one top scorer quickly found a workaround for a launch-blocking compiler bug); it 'helped us hire most of our current performance engineering team'; several top engineers hired from undergrad on its strength. Version 3: 'scores correlate well with the caliber of candidates' past work' (early, no r reported). No adverse impact or reliability data.
relevance_to_angle: Strongly supports 'stop testing convergent coding': a well-scored, convergent optimisation task stopped separating top humans from the model within a timed format. Complicates it too: Anthropic's response was not to drop the coding test for a design conversation, but to keep a coding take-home and move it out of distribution (novel puzzles), explicitly giving up realism. Supports 'working with an agent': AI is allowed because that is the job, and tooling judgement is scored. It also raises a problem for agent-directed tests, since if the model is better alone, 'the dominant strategy might become sitting back and watching'. Hume's list of what the job now is (debugging, systems design, verification, simplifying Claude's code) supports the design-judgement angle, but he says these are hard to test objectively in limited time. Nothing on communication or team fit.
limitations_stated: "Humans can still outperform models when given unlimited time." On version 3: "I'm still sad to have given up the realism and varied depth of the original. But realism may be a luxury we no longer have." Results are early ("Early results are promising"; "It might have lower variance than the original"). The real job's skills are "tough to test in an objective way without a lot of time or common context. It's always been hard to design interviews that represent the job, but now it's harder than ever." The durability of the fix is unknown: "We're curious how long it lasts." Attempt 1 failed because Claude could draw on 'a larger toolbox of experience' for well-known optimisation problems.
counter_evidence: Single company, single team, single role type (performance engineering), and the company sells the model being compared, so there is an incentive to present the model as matching top humans. The comparison is under a strict time limit; with unlimited time the best human beat the model, so 'cannot distinguish' is a property of the timed format, not of the people. One Opus 4.5 result required a human hint (the target cycle count). The best human in that comparison was themselves using Claude 4. Validity claims are anecdotal with no published coefficients. The redesign shows a coding take-home can be made AI-resistant again, which cuts against a claim that coding tests are obsolete, though Hume concedes it no longer resembles the job. Secondary coverage framed it as 'cheating', which TechCrunch had to correct.
verification_status: Checked against the primary Anthropic post (full text retrieved and searched): candidate count, Claude 3.7 Sonnet >50% figure, Opus 4 and Opus 4.5 results and conditions, the 'no longer had a way to distinguish' quote, rejection of an AI ban, AI-permitted policy, time limit change, version 3 design, benchmark cycle counts, validity anecdotes, closing line: all verified. Author role and 21 January 2026 date verified on the page.
